claim: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurological disorder characterized by motor disturbances.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurological disorder characterized by motor disturbances.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing HD as a neurological disorder with motor disturbances.

claim: HD pathology is most prominent in the striatum, the central hub of the basal ganglia.
source: HD pathology is most prominent in the striatum, the central hub of the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract about the primary location of HD pathology.

claim: Progressive cortico-striatal disconnection characterizes HD.
source: progressive cortico-striatal disconnection characterizes HD.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing a key feature of HD pathology.

claim: Multimodal MRI in vivo indicates cortico-striatal and thalamo-striatal functional network deficits in HD mice.
source: Multimodal MRI in vivo indicates cortico-striatal and thalamo-striatal functional network deficits and reduced glutamate/glutamine ratio in the striatum of HD mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract reporting findings from MRI experiments.

claim: HD mice show reduced glutamate/glutamine ratio in the striatum.
source: Multimodal MRI in vivo indicates cortico-striatal and thalamo-striatal functional network deficits and reduced glutamate/glutamine ratio in the striatum of HD mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract reporting MRI findings.

claim: Optogenetically-induced glutamate release from M2 cortex terminals in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) was undetectable in HD mice.
source: Moreover, optogenetically-induced glutamate release from M2 cortex terminals in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) was undetectable in HD mice and striatal neurons show blunted electrophysiological responses.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract reporting experimental findings from optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Striatal neurons show blunted electrophysiological responses in HD mice.
source: Moreover, optogenetically-induced glutamate release from M2 cortex terminals in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) was undetectable in HD mice and striatal neurons show blunted electrophysiological responses.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract reporting electrophysiological findings.

claim: Repeated M2-DLS optogenetic stimulation normalized motor behavior in HD mice.
source: Remarkably, repeated M2-DLS optogenetic stimulation normalized motor behavior in HD mice and evoked a sustained increase of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract reporting the effects of optogenetic stimulation on behavior.

claim: Repeated M2-DLS optogenetic stimulation evoked a sustained increase of synaptic plasticity in HD mice.
source: Remarkably, repeated M2-DLS optogenetic stimulation normalized motor behavior in HD mice and evoked a sustained increase of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract reporting the effects of optogenetic stimulation on synaptic plasticity.

claim: Selective stimulation of the M2-DLS pathway can become an effective therapeutic strategy in HD.
source: Overall, these results reveal that selective stimulation of the M2-DLS pathway can become an effective therapeutic strategy in HD.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract presenting the conclusion of the study.

claim: HD is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (Htt) gene.
source: HD is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (Htt) gene that translates into a polyglutamine tract in the Htt protein.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing the genetic cause of HD.

claim: The CAG repeat expansion translates into a polyglutamine tract in the Htt protein.
source: HD is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (Htt) gene that translates into a polyglutamine tract in the Htt protein.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing the molecular consequence of the CAG repeat expansion.

claim: Mutant Htt (mHtt) is expressed throughout the brain.
source: Mutant Htt (mHtt) is expressed throughout the brain and disrupts a wide range of molecular pathways and signaling cascades, yet HD pathology is most prominent in the basal ganglia circuitry.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction about the expression pattern of mutant huntingtin.

claim: Mutant Htt disrupts a wide range of molecular pathways and signaling cascades.
source: Mutant Htt (mHtt) is expressed throughout the brain and disrupts a wide range of molecular pathways and signaling cascades, yet HD pathology is most prominent in the basal ganglia circuitry.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction about the effects of mutant huntingtin.

claim: The striatum controls movements and behavior through a myriad of inputs and outputs.
source: The central hub of the basal ganglia is the striatum, which controls movements and behavior through a myriad of inputs and outputs (Calabresi et al., 2014; Freeze et al., 2013; Rothwell et al., 2015; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by multiple citations.

claim: The striatum receives glutamatergic inputs from all neocortical areas and the thalamus.
source: The striatum receives glutamatergic inputs from all neocortical areas and the thalamus (Bolam et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by a citation.

claim: Information flows from the cortex through the basal ganglia and goes back to the cortex via the thalamus through two main pathways (direct and indirect).
source: Information flows from the cortex through the basal ganglia and it goes back to the cortex via the thalamus through two main pathways (direct and indirect), which orchestrate the proper execution of movement.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing basal ganglia circuitry.

claim: The direct and indirect pathways orchestrate the proper execution of movement.
source: Information flows from the cortex through the basal ganglia and it goes back to the cortex via the thalamus through two main pathways (direct and indirect), which orchestrate the proper execution of movement.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction about the function of basal ganglia pathways.

claim: The specific origin of the cortical inputs to the striatum provides a substrate for information segregation in these circuits.
source: Additionally, the specific origin of the cortical inputs to the striatum provides a substrate for information segregation in these circuits (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by citations.

claim: Motor symptoms in HD emerge from dysregulated information flow through the basal ganglia circuits.
source: In HD, motor symptoms emerge from dysregulated information flow through the basal ganglia circuits.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction about the mechanism of motor symptoms in HD.

claim: Disturbances of the cortico-striatal communication have a leading role in HD network dysfunction.
source: Disturbances of the cortico-striatal communication have a leading role in HD network dysfunction, with alterations appearing in prodromal HD (Burgold et al., 2019; Dumas et al., 2013; Unschuld et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by citations.

claim: Alterations in cortico-striatal communication appear in prodromal HD.
source: Disturbances of the cortico-striatal communication have a leading role in HD network dysfunction, with alterations appearing in prodromal HD (Burgold et al., 2019; Dumas et al., 2013; Unschuld et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by citations.

claim: The caudate nucleus and the premotor cortex are predominantly affected in HD.
source: Specifically, the caudate nucleus and the premotor cortex are predominantly affected (Unschuld et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by a citation.

claim: There is a progressive disconnection between cortex and striatum in HD mouse models.
source: In HD mouse models, there is abundant evidence of a progressive disconnection between cortex and striatum (Cepeda et al., 2007; Veldman and Yang, 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by citations.

claim: Cortico-striatal dysfunction in HD is strongly supported by impaired cortico-striatal-dependent motor functions.
source: Cortico-striatal dysfunction in HD is strongly supported by the impaired cortico-striatal-dependent motor functions (Hong et al., 2012; Puigdellívol et al., 2015), altered paired-pulse facilitation at cortico-striatal synapses (Milnerwood and Raymond, 2007), reduction of striatal excitatory postsynaptic currents with loss of cortico-striatal synapses (Cepeda et al., 2003; Deng et al., 2013); and altered glutamate release in the striatum of transgenic R6/1 mice (Nicniocaill et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by multiple citations.

claim: HD shows altered paired-pulse facilitation at cortico-striatal synapses.
source: Cortico-striatal dysfunction in HD is strongly supported by the impaired cortico-striatal-dependent motor functions (Hong et al., 2012; Puigdellívol et al., 2015), altered paired-pulse facilitation at cortico-striatal synapses (Milnerwood and Raymond, 2007), reduction of striatal excitatory postsynaptic currents with loss of cortico-striatal synapses (Cepeda et al., 2003; Deng et al., 2013); and altered glutamate release in the striatum of transgenic R6/1 mice (Nicniocaill et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction supported by a citation.

claim: HD shows reduction of striatal excitatory postsynaptic currents with loss of cortico-striatal synapses.

claim: Transgenic R6/1 mice show altered glutamate release in the striatum.
source: Cortico-striatal dysfunction in HD is strongly supported by the impaired cortico-striatal-dependent motor functions (Hong et al., 2012; Puigdellívol et al., 2015), altered paired-pulse facilitation at cortico-striatal synapses (Milnerwood and Raymond, 2007), reduction of striatal excitatory postsynaptic currents with loss of cortico-striatal synapses (Cepeda et al., 2003; Deng et al., 2013); and altered glutamate release in the striatum of transgenic R6/1 mice (Nicniocaill et al., 2001).

claim: Reducing mHtt in the striatum is not sufficient to revert HD neurodegeneration.
source: Moreover, reducing mHtt in the striatum is not sufficient to revert HD neurodegeneration, while reducing mHtt expression in both striatum and cortex ameliorates behavioral and neuropathological features of HD animals (Gu et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: Reducing mHtt expression in both striatum and cortex ameliorates behavioral and neuropathological features of HD animals.

claim: A progressive disconnection of cortico-striatal pathways alters the information processing in basal ganglia circuitry, leading to motor disturbances.
source: Thus, a progressive disconnection of cortico-striatal pathways alters the information processing in basal ganglia circuitry, leading to motor disturbances.

claim: The reduced glutamate/glutamine ratio suggests a reduced glutamatergic release in the striatum of HD mice.

claim: GluCEST showed decreased glutamate levels in the striatum of HD mice compared to WT animals.
source: GluCEST showed decreased glutamate levels in the striatum and cortex of HD mice compared to WT animals, as shown by two-way ANOVA brain region effect (F(1,21) = 16.59; p = 0.0005), genotype effect (F(1,21) = 6.541; p = 0.0183) but not region/genotype interaction effect (F(1,21) = 3.286; p = 0.0842), and Bonferroni post hoc comparisons showed significant differences between WT and HD in both regions (Figure 2d–e).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting GluCEST findings.

claim: GluCEST showed decreased glutamate levels in the cortex of HD mice compared to WT animals.
source: GluCEST showed decreased glutamate levels in the striatum and cortex of HD mice compared to WT animals, as shown by two-way ANOVA brain region effect (F(1,21) = 16.59; p = 0.0005), genotype effect (F(1,21) = 6.541; p = 0.0183) but not region/genotype interaction effect (F(1,21) = 3.286; p = 0.0842), and Bonferroni post hoc comparisons showed significant differences between WT and HD in both regions (Figure 2d–e).

claim: A significant correlation between MRS and GluCEST was observed for all cases (r = 0.5979; p = 0.0026).

evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting correlation analysis.

claim: Extracellular glutamate concentration under baseline conditions was similar between WT and HD genotypes.
source: Extracellular glutamate concentration under baseline conditions, calculated as the mean of the first six collected samples, was similar between genotypes (WT: 0.73 ± 0.08; HD: 0.69 ± 0.06 pmol/sample).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting microdialysis findings.

claim: Blue light stimulation led to increased glutamate levels in WT-ChR2 mice.
source: Blue light stimulation led to increased glutamate levels in WT-ChR2, which returned to baseline levels after stimulation.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting microdialysis findings.

claim: Increases in glutamate level were not detected in HD-ChR2 mice during optogenetic stimulation.
source: However, increases in glutamate level were not detected in HD-ChR2 mice nor in the WT-YFP and HD-YFP control mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting microdialysis findings.

claim: The results indicate a reduced cortico-striatal-dependent glutamate release in symptomatic HD mice compared to WT controls.
source: These data indicate a reduced cortico-striatal-dependent glutamate release in symptomatic HD mice compared to WT controls.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results interpreting the microdialysis findings.

claim: Optic stimulation of M2 cortex afferent pathways evoked fPSC in the dorsal striatum.
source: We found that optic stimulation of M2 cortex afferent pathways evoked fPSC in the dorsal striatum (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting MEA findings.

claim: The amplitude of the evoked striatal fPSC was significantly larger in WT-ChR2 than in HD-ChR2 mice.
source: Two-way ANOVA showed that the amplitude of the evoked striatal fPSC was significantly larger in WT-ChR2 than in HD-ChR2 mouse (genotype effect; F(10,55) = 1.188; p = 0.0395) followed by Bonferroni post hoc comparisons.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting MEA findings.

claim: Increasing laser intensity led to fPSC of larger amplitude in both WT and HD mouse groups.
source: Also, increasing laser intensity led to fPSC of larger amplitude in both mouse groups (light intensity factor; F(10,55) = 9.906; p < 0.00001).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting MEA findings.

claim: The results confirm the reliability of the optogenetic approach as they provide evidence of a specific striatal response to the selective optogenetic activation of cortico-striatal afferents.

claim: The M2 cortex-DLS circuit in HD is functionally altered, possibly due to both pre- and postsynaptic effects.

claim: The total distance traveled was similar in all experimental groups during OF sessions.

claim: Exploratory behavior, measured as rearing time, was reduced in HD mice compared to WT.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation induced an increase of exploratory behavior over the sessions in HD-ChR2 mice.
source: Optogenetic stimulation induced an increase of exploratory behavior over the sessions in HD-ChR2 mice (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplements 2b and 3b).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting behavioral findings.

claim: HD mice showed an increased stereotypic behavior, as compared to WT mice.

claim: Repeated optogenetic stimulation reduced stereotypical behavior in HD-ChR2 mice.

claim: M2 cortex-DLS stimulation had a stronger impact on the modulation of spontaneous activity of HD mice, while acute locomotor activation was not observed.

claim: The effects of the light stimulation on exploratory behavior were manifested before and after stimulation over the sessions, suggesting some long-lasting effects evoked by the optogenetic stimulation of this M2-DLS circuit.

evidence: This is a direct statement from the results interpreting behavioral findings.

claim: HD mice showed reduced latency to fall compared to WT in the accelerating rotarod test.

evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting motor learning findings.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the M2 cortex-DLS pathway increased the latency to fall from the rod in HD-ChR2 mice to similar levels as WT mice.
source: Interestingly, optogenetic stimulation of the M2 cortex-DLS pathway increased the latency to fall from the rod in HD-ChR2 mice to similar levels as WT mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting motor learning findings.

claim: The number of 5 cm-frames crossed in the balance beam test was reduced in HD-YFP mice compared to WT mice.
source: The number of 5 cm-frames crossed was reduced in HD-YFP mice compared to WT mice, as already described (Creus-Muncunill et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting motor coordination findings.

claim: M2 cortex-DLS stimulation ameliorated motor coordination in HD-ChR2 mice, reaching similar levels to WT mice.
source: Remarkably, M2 cortex-DLS stimulation ameliorated motor coordination in HD-ChR2 mice, reaching similar levels to WT mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results reporting motor coordination findings.

claim: The prior activation of the M2-DLS circuit induces long-lasting effects that impact the basal ganglia motor function.
source: These data suggest that the prior activation of the M2-DLS circuit induces long-lasting effects that impact the basal ganglia motor function.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results interpreting motor behavior findings.

claim: By repeated activation of selected cortico-striatal circuits, that is, M2-DLS circuit, we can successfully ameliorate motor function in HD.

claim: Repeated optogenetic stimulation increased spine density in HD mice.
